This section outlines our experimental setup. We evaluate five models from two model families (Llama and Qwen) across six precision settings on five benchmarks. Additional details are in $\ S \mathrm { A }$

Models: We evaluate five open-weight models from two families: Llama 3.1 8B and 70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen 2.5 7B, 32B, and 72B (Qwen, 2024c; Yang et al., 2024)． All models support up to 128K input tokens.3

Quantization methods:We use BF16 as the fullprecision baseline and compare four quantization methods at 4-bit and 8-bit precisions against it:

1. AWQ: 4-bit integer (W4A16)4 quantization (Lin et al., 2024), referred to as AWQ-int4.   
2. BNB: 4-bit floating-point quantization using bitsandbytes (W4A16) (Dettmers et al., 2023), referred to as BNB-nf4.   
3. GPTQ: (a) 4-bit integer (W4A16), referred to as GPTQ-int4,and (b) 8-bit integer (W8A16), referred to as GPTQ-int8 (Frantar et al., 2023).   
4. FP8: Dynamic 8-bit floating-point quantization (W8A8) (Micikevicius et al., 2022), referred to as FP8.

In total, we benchmark five models across five quantization setups and the BF16 baselines, resulting in 3O configurations.

Inference setup:All models are run using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on one to four A100-80G GPUs,except for the FP8 models,which require H100 GPUs due to the lack of FP8 support on A100 (vLLM, 2024). All experiments use greedy decoding with a temperature of O.O to ensure deterministic outputs.

Benchmark tasks: The BF16 models and their quantized variants are evaluated on five benchmarks:(1) RULER(Hsieh et al., 2O24a) for English long-context retrieval, (2) ONERULER (Kim et al., 2O25) for long-context retrieval across languages, (3) NoCHA (Karpinska et al., 2024) for long-context reasoning，(4) FAcTScoRE (Min et al., 2O23) for factual biography generation,and (5) CS4 (Atmakuru et al., 2024) for constrained creative story generation. The first three tasks evaluate model performance on long inputs,while the last two focus on long-form outputs. See $\ S _ { \mathbf { B } }$ for more details.

candidate_windows.section_title: statistical tests of significance for comparing quantization methods
candidate_windows.normalized_section_title: statistical tests of significance for comparing quantization methods
candidate_windows.window_text:
We conducted statistical analysis by fiting the generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) using the glmer(） function from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2O15) to study if different quantization methods performed significantly differently from their BF16 counterparts. For improved convergence,we used a binomial logit link and the bobyqa optimizer. We formatted our data in long format, with each model response represented as a binary categorical variable indicating whether the prediction was correct or incorrect. Quantization methods were included as the primary fixed effect of interest, with additional fixed effects for context length, task,and their interactions in different model variants. For each GLMM we report marginal $R ^ { 2 }$ ，the variance explained by fixed effects alone,and conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ , the variance explained by fixed and random effects (Nakagawa et al., 2017). We also list the variance components $( \sigma ^ { 2 } , \tau _ { 0 0 } )$ and intraclass correlation coeficients (ICC) for every grouping factor. Other aspects like task, context length, and language are added where appropriate to account for the non-independence of repeated measures and to allow the fixed effects of interest to be estimated after partialing out systematic differences due solely to model identity, task, or input length. Following (Karpinska et al.， 2024)，we conducted pairwise comparisons of quantization levels with emmeans for every GLMM. p-values were Bonferroni-adjusted (Westfall et al., 1997) and reported in the post-hoc tables.Log-odds estimates were exponentiated to odds ratios,which were then converted to probabilities to facilitate interpretation (a probability of 0.5O means the two methods are equally accurate). To examine how quantization interacts with context length and task type within RULER, we fit three GLMMs with Model as a random intercept. The main-effect model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $^ +$ （1|Model)） tests whether any quantization method differs from BF16 (Table 3; pairwise contrasts in Table 4). The interaction model with context length (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Context_length $^ +$ (1|Model) $^ +$ (1 |Task)) evaluates whether quantization effects vary across $^ \mathrm { 8 k }$ ,64k,and $1 2 8 \mathrm { k }$ tokens while controlling for task variability (Table 5;contrasts in Table 6). The task interaction model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Task $^ + ($ 1|Model)） compares performance of quantized models on multikey and multi-value tasks on RULER,using BF16 on needle as the reference (Table 7; contrasts in Table 8). Across these models, marginal $R ^ { 2 }$ increases from .013 (quantization only) to .615 (quantization \* context-length),while conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ peaks at .488,indicating that both fixed effects and grouping factors jointly capture a sizeable proportion of variance on RULER. We conduct the same statistical analyses with ONERULERas in RULER（Tables 9 to 14), with the only change being the use of language frequency instead of task. NoCHA analyses parallel the RULER tests but center on the $7 5 \mathrm { k }$ -token split defined in the benchmark. The main-effect model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $^ +$ （1|Context_length） $^ +$ (1|Model)） includes quantization as the predictor, with Context_length and Model as random intercepts (Table 15)； pairwise contrasts appear in Table 16. To test whether quantization errors increase for longer inputs,we also fit an interaction model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Context_length $^ +$ （1|Model)),using BF16 at $\le 7 5 \mathrm { k }$ tokens as the reference (Table 17; contrast results are reported in Table 18). Random-effects variances are small for NoCHA $( I C C _ { \mathrm { { M o d e l } } } ~ \approx$ 0.045),and both marginal and conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ values are low $( \approx 0 . 0 1 6 )$ , indicating the dataset's overall difficulty. To evaluate how quantization impacts performance on FACTScORE, we fit three linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models with Model as a random intercept. The main-effect model (log_veriscore $\sim$ Quantization $^ +$ (1|topic) $^ +$ （1|Model)） estimates whether quantized models deviate from the BF16 baseline in overall generation quality (Table 19； pairwise contrasts in Table 2O). To assess no claim rate,we model the likelihood of no claims (glmer(no_claims $\sim$ Quantization $+ ( 1 | \mathsf { M o d e l } ) + ( 1 | \mathsf { t o p i c } ) ) )$ in Table 21 with contrasts in Table 22. Lastly, we examine whether quantization interacts with category(log_veriscore $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ （ $\mathsf { \Lambda } \mathsf { z } \mathsf { a } \mathsf { t } ~ + ~ ( 1 \mathsf { | M o d e l } ) ~ + ~ ( 1 \mathsf { | t o p i c } )$ bymodeling VERIScORE across medium, very frequent, and very rare categories (Table 23; post-hoc contrasts in Table 24). Figure 26 in $\ S { \bf C } . 5$ plots the absolute constraint satisfaction scores of each model-quantization pair. Here,we fit GLMMs to evaluate how quantization influences constraint satisfaction on CS4. However,each data point here reflects the percentage of constraints satisfied,i.e., a success proportion,rather than a binary label. Since this can only take a finite set of values,we use a binomial GLMM with cbind. The main-effect model (cbind(Success，Failures) $\sim$ Quantization +（1|Model)） tests whether quantized models differ from BF16 in satisfying constraints (Table 25; pairwise contrasts in Table 26). To analyze whether quantization interacts with the number of input constraints,we introduce input-level interactions in (cbind(Success，Failures) $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Input_constraints $^ +$ （1|Model)),allowing us to track performance across 7,23,and 39 input constraints (Table 27; post-hoc results in Table 28). This section outlines our experimental setup. We evaluate five models from two model families (Llama and Qwen) across six precision settings on five benchmarks. Additional details are in $\ S \mathrm { A }$

Models: We evaluate five open-weight models from two families: Llama 3.1 8B and 70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen 2.5 7B, 32B, and 72B (Qwen, 2024c; Yang et al., 2024)． All models support up to 128K input tokens.3

Quantization methods:We use BF16 as the fullprecision baseline and compare four quantization methods at 4-bit and 8-bit precisions against it:

1. AWQ: 4-bit integer (W4A16)4 quantization (Lin et al., 2024), referred to as AWQ-int4.   
2. BNB: 4-bit floating-point quantization using bitsandbytes (W4A16) (Dettmers et al., 2023), referred to as BNB-nf4.   
3. GPTQ: (a) 4-bit integer (W4A16), referred to as GPTQ-int4,and (b) 8-bit integer (W8A16), referred to as GPTQ-int8 (Frantar et al., 2023).   
4. FP8: Dynamic 8-bit floating-point quantization (W8A8) (Micikevicius et al., 2022), referred to as FP8.

In total, we benchmark five models across five quantization setups and the BF16 baselines, resulting in 3O configurations.

Inference setup:All models are run using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on one to four A100-80G GPUs,except for the FP8 models,which require H100 GPUs due to the lack of FP8 support on A100 (vLLM, 2024). All experiments use greedy decoding with a temperature of O.O to ensure deterministic outputs.

Benchmark tasks: The BF16 models and their quantized variants are evaluated on five benchmarks:(1) RULER(Hsieh et al., 2O24a) for English long-context retrieval, (2) ONERULER (Kim et al., 2O25) for long-context retrieval across languages, (3) NoCHA (Karpinska et al., 2024) for long-context reasoning，(4) FAcTScoRE (Min et al., 2O23) for factual biography generation,and (5) CS4 (Atmakuru et al., 2024) for constrained creative story generation. The first three tasks evaluate model performance on long inputs,while the last two focus on long-form outputs. See $\ S _ { \mathbf { B } }$ for more details.

# Appendix

# AExperimental setup: additional details

# A.1Obtaining quantized models

Our objective was to study how easily available quantized models handle long-context and longform tasks. So,we primarily relied on quantized models provided widely by RedHat AI (former NeuralMagic; (Kurtic et al.， 2024), HuggingQuants,and Qwen-2.5's official repository, since these are popular resources for quantized versions of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5, with up to $3 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ downloads as of July 2025.

Table 1 provides an overview of how quantized models were obtained for this study. Some specifics are detailed below.

For Llama-3.1 70B, we observed noticeable accuracy degradation upon using the default GPTQint8 (W8A16) quantization recipe. Kurtic et al. (2024) encountered the same issue with the W8A8 version and resolved it by integrating SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) into their W8A8 GPTQ-int8 recipe. We use this same quantization recipe from Kurtic et al. (2024) and performed a W8A16 GPTQ-int8 quantization, by which we were able to largely retain the pre-quantization accuracy.

For Qwen-2.5 models, FP8-Dynamic models were created locally using LLMCompressor (Shaw et al., 2024; NeuralMagic, 2024), borrowing the same quantization recipe used by Kurtic et al. (2024) for Llama-3.1.

For BNB-nf4, we use in-flight quantization directly from the full-precision checkpoints (vLLM, 2024). We launch vLLM with quantization=bitsandbytes. This converts BF16 weights to nf4 blocks at load time,and then runs inference by de-quantizing those blocks on-chip before each GEMM, while activations remain in BF16. We do not experiment with the 8-bit integer BNB quantization (Dettmers et al.,2022) since it is not supported on vLLM.14

# A.2Using Qwen-2.5 for long context tasks:

Though Qwen-2.5 has a context length of 128K, the default configuration is set to support context lengths only up to 32K; for longer contexts, the official Qwen documentation (Qwen, 2024b) suggests employing YARN (Peng et al., 2024) to extrapolate the RoPE scaling and achieve $4 \times$ the context length. We adopt the same approach and modify Qwen model configuration when running on context lengths larger than 32K.

# A.3 Computational Cost

We estimate the approximate compute consumption as follows: NoCHA: 180O hours,RULER: 500 hours, ONERULER: 3200 hours, CS4: 180 hours, and FAcTScORE: 1OO hours, totaling roughly 5800 GPU hours on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

review_flags.section_title: statistical tests of significance for comparing quantization methods
review_flags.evidence:
We conducted statistical analysis by fiting the generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) using the glmer(） function from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2O15) to study if different quantization methods performed significantly differently from their BF16 counterparts. For improved convergence,we used a binomial logit link and the bobyqa optimizer. We formatted our data in long format, with each model response represented as a binary categorical variable indicating whether the prediction was correct or incorrect. Quantization methods were included as the primary fixed effect of interest, with additional fixed effects for context length, task,and their interactions in different model variants. For each GLMM we report marginal $R ^ { 2 }$ ，the variance explained by fixed effects alone,and conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ , the variance explained by fixed and random effects (Nakagawa et al., 2017). We also list the variance components $( \sigma ^ { 2 } , \tau _ { 0 0 } )$ and intraclass correlation coeficients (ICC) for every grouping factor. Other aspects like task, context length, and language are added where appropriate to account for the non-independence of repeated measures and to allow the fixed effects of interest to be estimated after partialing out systematic differences due solely to model identity, task, or input length. Following (Karpinska et al.， 2024)，we conducted pairwise comparisons of quantization levels with emmeans for every GLMM. p-values were Bonferroni-adjusted (Westfall et al., 1997) and reported in the post-hoc tables.Log-odds estimates were exponentiated to odds ratios,which were then converted to probabilities to facilitate interpretation (a probability of 0.5O means the two methods are equally accurate). To examine how quantization interacts with context length and task type within RULER, we fit three GLMMs with Model as a random intercept. The main-effect model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $^ +$ （1|Model)） tests whether any quantization method differs from BF16 (Table 3; pairwise contrasts in Table 4). The interaction model with context length (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Context_length $^ +$ (1|Model) $^ +$ (1 |Task)) evaluates whether quantization effects vary across $^ \mathrm { 8 k }$ ,64k,and $1 2 8 \mathrm { k }$ tokens while controlling for task variability (Table 5;contrasts in Table 6). The task interaction model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Task $^ + ($ 1|Model)） compares performance of quantized models on multikey and multi-value tasks on RULER,using BF16 on needle as the reference (Table 7; contrasts in Table 8). Across these models, marginal $R ^ { 2 }$ increases from .013 (quantization only) to .615 (quantization \* context-length),while conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ peaks at .488,indicating that both fixed effects and grouping factors jointly capture a sizeable proportion of variance on RULER. We conduct the same statistical analyses with ONERULERas in RULER（Tables 9 to 14), with the only change being the use of language frequency instead of task. NoCHA analyses parallel the RULER tests but center on the $7 5 \mathrm { k }$ -token split defined in the benchmark. The main-effect model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $^ +$ （1|Context_length） $^ +$ (1|Model)） includes quantization as the predictor, with Context_length and Model as random intercepts (Table 15)； pairwise contrasts appear in Table 16. To test whether quantization errors increase for longer inputs,we also fit an interaction model (Binary_label $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Context_length $^ +$ （1|Model)),using BF16 at $\le 7 5 \mathrm { k }$ tokens as the reference (Table 17; contrast results are reported in Table 18). Random-effects variances are small for NoCHA $( I C C _ { \mathrm { { M o d e l } } } ~ \approx$ 0.045),and both marginal and conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ values are low $( \approx 0 . 0 1 6 )$ , indicating the dataset's overall difficulty. To evaluate how quantization impacts performance on FACTScORE, we fit three linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models with Model as a random intercept. The main-effect model (log_veriscore $\sim$ Quantization $^ +$ (1|topic) $^ +$ （1|Model)） estimates whether quantized models deviate from the BF16 baseline in overall generation quality (Table 19； pairwise contrasts in Table 2O). To assess no claim rate,we model the likelihood of no claims (glmer(no_claims $\sim$ Quantization $+ ( 1 | \mathsf { M o d e l } ) + ( 1 | \mathsf { t o p i c } ) ) )$ in Table 21 with contrasts in Table 22. Lastly, we examine whether quantization interacts with category(log_veriscore $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ （ $\mathsf { \Lambda } \mathsf { z } \mathsf { a } \mathsf { t } ~ + ~ ( 1 \mathsf { | M o d e l } ) ~ + ~ ( 1 \mathsf { | t o p i c } )$ bymodeling VERIScORE across medium, very frequent, and very rare categories (Table 23; post-hoc contrasts in Table 24). Figure 26 in $\ S { \bf C } . 5$ plots the absolute constraint satisfaction scores of each model-quantization pair. Here,we fit GLMMs to evaluate how quantization influences constraint satisfaction on CS4. However,each data point here reflects the percentage of constraints satisfied,i.e., a success proportion,rather than a binary label. Since this can only take a finite set of values,we use a binomial GLMM with cbind. The main-effect model (cbind(Success，Failures) $\sim$ Quantization +（1|Model)） tests whether quantized models differ from BF16 in satisfying constraints (Table 25; pairwise contrasts in Table 26). To analyze whether quantization interacts with the number of input constraints,we introduce input-level interactions in (cbind(Success，Failures) $\sim$ Quantization $\star$ Input_constraints $^ +$ （1|Model)),allowing us to track performance across 7,23,and 39 input constraints (Table 27; post-hoc results in Table 28). # Does quantization affect models’ performance on long-context tasks?

Anmol Mekala\*2 Anirudh Atmakuru\*2 {amekala， aatmakuru}@umass.edu Yixiao Song2Marzena Karpinska\*Mohit Iyyer2 yixiaosong@umass.edumkarpinska@microsoft.commiyyer@umd.edu 2UMass Amherst\*MicrosoftUniversity of Maryland, Collge Park

# Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) now support context windows exceeding 128K tokens, but this comes with significant memory requirements and high inference latency. Quantization can mitigate these costs, but may degrade performance.In this work, we present the first systematic evaluation of quantized LLMs on tasks with long inputs ( ${ \geq } 6 4 \mathrm { K }$ tokens）and long-form outputs. Our evaluation spans 9.7K test examples, five quantization methods (FP8, GPTQint8,AWQ-int4, GPTQ-int4, BNB-nf4),and five models (Llama-3.1 8B and 70B; Qwen-2.5 7B,32B,and 72B).We find that, on average, 8-bit quantization preserves accuracy $( \sim 0 . 8 \%$ drop),whereas 4-bit methods lead to substantial losses,especially for tasks involving longcontext inputs (drops of up to $5 9 \%$ ). This degradation tends to worsen when the input is in a language other than English． Crucially,the effects of quantization depend heavily on the quantization method,model,and task.For instance,while Qwen-2.5 72B remains robust under BNB-nf4,Llama-3.1 7OB experiences a $32 \%$ performance drop on the same task. These findings highlight the importance of a careful, task-specific evaluation before deploying quantized LLMs,particularly in long-context scenarios and for languages other than English.

github.com/molereddy/long-context-quantization

# 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) serve a vast community of users through APIs and web services. However, their inference demands substantial resources,severely constraining scalability and increasing energy consumption (Samsi et al., 2023; Luccioni et al., 2024; Fernandez et al., 2025). Posttraining quantization aims to solve this problem by approximating models at lower precision (Zhou et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024). 8-bit quantization (Micikevicius et al., 2022; Frantar et al., 2023) provides accuracy at half the cost, and more aggressive 4-bit approaches (Lin et al., 2024; Dettmers et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2023) offer even greater cost-effectiveness.Model providers widely offer quantized models (Meta AI, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024; Databricks, 2023), but the impact on performance has not been explored exhaustively.

While previous work has shown that quantized LLMs largely maintain performance on standard benchmarks (Badshah and Sajjad, 2O24; Liu et al., 2024b; Jin et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024, inter alia), these studies have mainly focused on tasks with short-form inputs and outputs (Jin et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2O24), rarely exceeding 2K input and 100 output tokens. This limited scope leaves open a critical gap: the impact of quantization on tasks requiring long-context inputs or long-form outputs.1 This is particularly salient because, as context length increases, the associated memory and compute requirements grow quadratically, making low-precision methods particularly attractive for effciency. Moreover, many modern LLMs now support context windows of 128K tokens or more, allowing them to process entire codebases, legal documents,or full novels. Such models,when aggressively quantized (e.g., to 4 bits), could theoretically handle significantly more context under the same memory budget.

However, to our knowledge, only Kurtic et al. (2024） have benchmarked long-context performance,and their study was confined to the RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024a) dataset. Critically, they only reported a single,aggregated score and did not provide a breakdown of performance at different context lengths,which can mask significant performance drops on very long inputs.

To address this gap,we conduct a systematic analysis of quantization performance across multiple models, quantization methods,and benchmark tasks. This includes five datasets across 9.7K test examples,with key factors varying such as context length, language, and output constraints. We evaluate five quantization methods (FP8, GPTQint8,AWQ-int4, GPTQ-int4,and BNB-NF4) on five models (Llama-3.1 8B and 70B; Qwen-2.5 7B, 32B,and 72B), comparing against their BF16 baselines. For long-context input tasks,we use RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024a) and ONERULER(Kim et al., 2025) to assess retrieval, and NoCHA (Karpinska et al.， 2024） to test reasoning over book-length texts. # 2Experimental setup

 

# Dataset:RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024a)

自Task:RULER evaluates model's effective context window with needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) retrieval tasks in English. The model must locate one or more target key-value pairs (the “needles") hidden in passages of varying lengths (the “haystacks"). Following Yen et al. (2025), the task includes three variants: (1) multi-key needle, (2) multi-key UUID,and (3) multi-value.Each variant is tested at three context lengths (8K, 64K,and 128K),’ with emphasis on longer contexts (64K and 128K).Each {task，context-length} combination includes 1OO examples, yielding 900 test examples in total.

√Metric: Following (Hsieh et al., 2024a), performance is measured using exact match accuracy against the gold answer.

# Dataset: ONERULER (Kim et al., 2025)

自Task:ONERULER extends RULER by evaluating NIAH retrieval tasks not only in English but also across multiple other languages.It also introduces no-needle scenarios,where models must explicitly predict the absence of a needle. ONERULER serves as an important complement to RULER in light of the performance degradation of quantized models observed by Marchisio et al. (2024) on non-Latin scripts.Each model is evaluated on two tasks (NIAH-single and NIAHnone; see $\ S \mathbf { B }$ ),three context lengths (8K,64K, and 128K), and 26 languages.Each {task, context-length， language} combination consists of 50 examples, totaling 7,800 test examples.

Metric:As with RULER, exact match accuracy is used as the metric.

Dataset: NoCHA (Karpinska et al., 2024)

自Task:NoCHA evaluates long-context reasoning by asking models to verify claims against book-length contexts. Each example includes a minimal pair of true and false claims with subtle but meaningful differences. Models are prompted to explain their reasoning before making a decision. T

自Task:NoCHA evaluates long-context reasoning by asking models to verify claims against book-length contexts. Each example includes a minimal pair of true and false claims with subtle but meaningful differences. Models are prompted to explain their reasoning before making a decision. The effect of quantization varies with model and task. Our results demonstrate that quantization effects are highly context-dependent, varying significantly with both model family and the evaluation task. This model-specific behavior is evident even between models of comparable size. On the ONERULER benchmark,for example, BNBnf4 quantization leads to a $59 \%$ accuracy drop for Llama-3.1 7OB,whereas the similarly-sized Qwen$2 . 5 ~ 7 2 \mathrm { B }$ gains $0 . 6 \%$ with the same method (Figure 6b). Sensitivity also varies within a model family; the Llama-3.1 models are generally more affected by quantization than the Qwen-2.5 models, whose larger 32B and 72B variants show higher resilience.13 This effect can even be unpredictable, as seen when BNB-nf4 causes a $32 \%$ performance drop on Llama-3.1 70B but a $0 . 6 \%$ gain on Llama3.1 8B (Figure 11).

Furthermore,a model's robustness to quantization is also task-dependent. For instance, that same Llama-3.1 7OB model, when quantized with GPTQ-int8, drops $1 1 . 1 \%$ on NoCHA (Figure 6c) but shows no comparable decline on RULER or ONERULER (Figure 6a, Figure 6b). These findings differ from prior work that examined a single model family and observed only minor performance drops (Kurtic et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2024), highlighting the importance of evaluating a diverse set of models.

# 4Related works

Prior studies on quantization effects: Recent work shows that 8-bit quantization preserves performance, while 4-bit methods incur only marginal accuracy loss (Kurtic et al., 2O24; Badshah and Sajjad,2024; Lu et al.,2024b; Jin et al.,2024; Huang et al.,2024; Xu et al.,2024; Li et al.,2024; del Rey et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). Lee et al. (2024) and Kurtic et al. (2O24) investigate Llama-3.1 and find that FP8 is nearly lossless,while AWQ-int4 and GPTQ-int4 exhibit small degradations, particularly in reasoning,coding tasks and on Arena-Hard. Results on Mistral (Badshah and Sajjad, 2024), Baichuan (Liu et al., 2024b),and Qwen-Chat (Jin et al., 2024) are also similar, with losses rarely exceeding $3 \%$ and diminishing as model size grows. Results on safety, alignment, and interpretability suggest that 4-bit quantization may (Egashira et al., 2024) or may not (Xu et al., 2024) lead to drops in safety, protect against data-poisoning (Hussain et al.,2O25)，reverse unlearning (Zhang et al., 2025),and have mixed results on interpretability (Wang et al., 2025b). Some studies have also shown that models are robust to quantization even at 3-bit precision or lower (Chee et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Egiazarian et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2025).However, these evaluations are generally limited in terms of the input context or the output token ranges,leaving longer-range effects unknown. A significant body of work has studied accuracy trade-offs using different quantization methods on academic benchmarks (Yao et al., 2024; Liu et al., $2 0 2 4 \mathrm { a }$ ; Gong et al., 2024a,b). However, these benchmarks may not fully reflect performance in realistic scenarios, such as those involving long-form reasoning or multilingual settings.For instance,Li et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2025) report significant drops for GPTQ-int4 and AWQ-int4 on such tasks. For multilingual LLMs, Marchisio et al. (2024) observe increasing drops on reasoning for non-Latin script languages upon quantization. We develop this picture further by evaluating long-form generation (CS4, FAcTScoRE) and across languages in ONERULER.

(2O24） evaluate quantization on long-context tasks, and they report coarse averages over RULER(which includes context lengths as low as 8K) to conclude negligible performance loss. Our analysis differs by focusing on the effects of parameters like context length, task-type, especially at context lengths ${ > } 6 4 \mathrm { K }$ . While they evaluate only the Llama-3.1 family and use a single 4- bit quantization (GPTQ-int4), we extend the scale of long context analysis by including ONERULER and NoCHA, the Qwen-2.5 model family, and the AWQ-int4 and BNB-nf4 quantizations. We find that Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.1 respond to quantization very differently,with Llama-3.1 showing larger drops upon quantization (Figure 6a). In addition, the AWQ-int4 quantization performs better than GPTQ-int4,while the popular BNB-nf4 quantization performs worse (Figure 3).

# 5Conclusion

In this paper, we presented a systematic evaluation of the performance of five open-weight models (7B to 72B parameters) across five quantization methods (4-bit and 8-bit). We conducted experiments on five tasks requiring the models to either process long-context inputs (in English or other languages) or return long-form outputs in English. While prior work often suggests 8-bit quantization is nearly lossless and 4-bit methods are good enough, our findings demonstrate that the impact of quantization becomes more pronounced in long-context scenarios. In particular, we observed that model's performance under 4-bit quantization tends to degrade progressively as input context length increases. 4- bit quantization has a significant impact when the input is in a language other than English. In contrast, 8-bit precision methods largely preserve accuracy across context lengths. Furthermore,we observed considerable heterogeneity in quantization effects-the performance impact of reduced precision varies significantly across different model architectures and task types. Taken together, these results indicate that quantization should be applied with careful consideration in long-context applications and in multilingual setups.

# Limitations

While we conduct a large-scale evaluation of quantized LLMs on long-context and long-form tasks, we identify the following limitations and hope future work will improve on these aspects to enable more comprehensive evaluations of quantization methods.

Scope of experiments: Our evaluations cover five quantization methods and five LLMs, with the largest model having 72 billion parameters. We largely followed publicly available,off-the-shelf quantized models and recipes (e.g., from the official Qwen repository, HuggingQuants,and NeuralMagic) and did not explore tuning each quantization method further. As a result, our findings might not fully generalize to other models or to quantization techniques beyond those tes

ailable,off-the-shelf quantized models and recipes (e.g., from the official Qwen repository, HuggingQuants,and NeuralMagic) and did not explore tuning each quantization method further. As a result, our findings might not fully generalize to other models or to quantization techniques beyond those tested.

Evaluation methodology and limited output lengths:Although we tested input contexts as long as 128K tokens,we restricted the generated outputs in our experiments to relatively short passages ( $( < 6 5 0$ tokens).We made this choice because our evaluation relies solely on automated metrics and LLM-based judge models,which are not reliable for evaluating very long text. Consequently, without human annotations, our assessment may overlook subtle errors in logical flow or nuanced instruction-following behavior over long-form outputs.

# A.1Obtaining quantized models

Our objective was to study how easily available quantized models handle long-context and longform tasks. So,we primarily relied on quantized models provided widely by RedHat AI (former NeuralMagic; (Kurtic et al.， 2024), HuggingQuants,and Qwen-2.5's official repository, since these are popular resources for quantized versions of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5, with up to $3 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ downloads as of July 2025.

Table 1 provides an overview of how quantized models were obtained for this study. Some specifics are detailed below.

For Llama-3.1 70B, we observed noticeable accuracy degradation upon using the default GPTQint8 (W8A16) quantization recipe. Kurtic et al. (2024) encountered the same issue with the W8A8 version and resolved it by integrating SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) into their W8A8 GPTQ-int8 recipe. We use this same quantization recipe from Kurtic et al. (2024) and performed a W8A16 GPTQ-int8 quantization, by which we were able to largely retain the pre-quantization accuracy.

For Qwen-2.5 models, FP8-Dynamic models were created locally using LLMCompressor (Shaw et al., 2024; NeuralMagic, 2024), borrowing the same quantization recipe used by Kurtic et al. (2024) for Llama-3.1.

For BNB-nf4, we use in-flight quantization directly from the full-precision checkpoints (vLLM, 2024). We launch vLLM with quantization=bitsandbytes. This converts BF16 weights to nf4 blocks at load time,and then runs inference by de-quantizing those blocks on-chip before each GEMM, while activations remain in BF16. We do not experiment with the 8-bit integer BNB quantization (Dettmers et al.,2022) since it is not supported on vLLM.14

# A.2Using Qwen-2.5 for long context tasks:

Though Qwen-2.5 has a context length of 128K, the default configuration is set to support context lengths only up to 32K; for longer contexts, the official Qwen documentation (Qwen, 2024b) suggests employing YARN (Peng et al., 2024) to extrapolate the RoPE scaling and achieve $4 \times$ the context length. We adopt the same approach and modify Qwen model configuration when running on context lengths larger than 32K.

# A.3 Computational Cost

We estimate the approximate compute consumption as follows: NoCHA: 180O hours,RULER: 500 hours, ONERULER: 3200 hours, CS4: 180 hours, and FAcTScORE: 1OO hours, totaling roughly 5800 GPU hours on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

,adding to the description in $\ S 2$ RULER: While Kurtic et al. (2O24) evaluate quantized LLMs on RULER and report coarse-grained, aggregated results across quantized models and context lengths,we perform a more detailed analysis. We follow Yen et al. (2025) to select our datapoints for the multi-key needle,multi-key UUID, and multi-value tasks from the RULER benchmark. In the multi-key task, the model must retrieve the value associated with a specific key given in the query,while ignoring others which serve as distractors. The multi-key UUID task tests a similar ability, but the values are 32-character longform strings (UUIDs),making it harder to match or guess, testing the model's ability to precisely extract the correct value without partial matching. Finally, the multi-value task increases the difficulty further by requiring the models to retrieve multiple values associated with the same key in the haystack. While the tokenizers for Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5 differ, Yen et al. (2025) use Llama-3.1 tokenizer to tokenize and construct their benchmark. This implies that Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5 receive slightly different numbers of input tokens for the same input datapoint. ONERULER: This benchmark extends RULER in two significant Ways. First, ONERULER's NIAH task includes points without any correct needle present, requiring models to abstain appropriately. Second, ONERULER expands the task beyond English to encompass 26 languages representing diverse language families and writing systems. They find that accuracy on NIAH shows large drops on low-resource languages, especially ones that use non-Latin scripts. We evaluate models using two NIAH task types: NIAH-single and NIAH-none. In NIAH-single, a single correct needle is present without distractors,which models must retrieve accurately. In NIAH-none,no correct needle is present, but four distractor needles exist, requiring models to abstain from retrieving any needle.

NoCHA: NoCHA evaluates long-context reasoning abilities by testing realistic claim verification and reasoning skills of LLMs on book-length texts. Since Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5 support context lengths of up to 128K tokens, this work considers the subset of datapoints with contexts up to that length, yielding 723 claim pairs drawn from 46 novels and three short story collections.While RULER and ONERULER help analyze the impact of quantization across varying context lengths, NoCHA enables a more nuanced investigation. First, it poses a significantly more challenging task for LLMs，with full-precision models from Llama3.1 and Qwen-2.5 performing at approximately chance level (Karpinska et al., 2O24). Additionally, NoCHA facilitates further analysis through various dataset splits.A split based on true versus false claims enables the study of potential LLMbiases. A difficulty-based split allows for examining the impact of question difficulty,and not just context length. Finally, a reasoning-scope-based split supports analysis across different spans of context required for reasoning. FACTScoRE: Evaluation procedure: the VERIScORE metric runs a three-stage evaluation pipeline: it extracts individual claims from the text using a task-finetuned LLM, focusing specifically ongenerating sensible and verifiable factual claims.It then retrieves evidence for each claim through Google search results using the Serper API.15 Finally, each claim is verified against the retrieved evidence using another task-finetuned LLM. To account for the open-ended nature of the generation, it computes the F1 score at K,where K is the median number of claims extracted across all responses. # FStatistical tests of significance for comparing quantization methods

We conducted statistical analysis by fiting the generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) using the glmer(） function from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2O15) to study if different quantization methods performed significantly differently from their BF16 counterparts. For improved convergence,we used a binomial logit link and the bobyqa optimizer. We formatted our data in long format, with each model response represented as a binary categorical variable indicating whether the prediction was correct or incorrect. Quantization methods were included as the primary fixed effect of interest, with additional fixed effects for context length, task,and their interactions in different model variants.

For each GLMM we report marginal $R ^ { 2 }$ ，the variance explained by fixed effects alone,and conditional $R ^ { 2 }$ , the variance explained by fixed and random effects (Nakagawa et al., 2017). We also list the variance components $( \sigma ^ { 2 } , \tau _ { 0 0 } )$ and intraclass correlation coeficients (ICC) for every grouping factor. Other aspects like task, context length, and language are added where appropriate to account for the non-independence of repeated measures and to allow the fixed effects of interest to be estimated after partialing out systematic differences due solely to model identity, task, or input length.

Following (Karpinska et al.， 2024)，we conducted pairwise comparisons of quantization levels with emmeans for every GLMM. p-values were Bonferroni-adjusted (Westfall et al., 1997) and reported in the post-hoc tables.Log-odds estimates were exponentiated to odds ratios,which were then converted to probabilities to facilitate interpretation (a probability of 0.5O means the two methods are equally accurate).

# Appendix

# AExperimental setup: additional details

# A.1Obtaining quantized models

Our objective was to study how easily available quantized models handle long-context and longform tasks. So,we primarily relied on quantized models provided widely by RedHat AI (former NeuralMagic; (Kurtic et al.， 2024), HuggingQuants,and Qwen-2.5's official repository, since these are popular resources for quantized versions of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5, with up to $3 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ downloads as of July 2025.

Table 1 provides an overview of how quantized models were obtained for this study. Some specifics are detailed below.

For Llama-3.1 70B, we observed noticeable accuracy degradation upon using the default GPTQint8 (W8A16) quantization recipe. Kurtic et al. (2024) encountered the same issue with the W8A8 version and resolved it by integrating SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) into their W8A8 GPTQ-int8 recipe. We use this same quantization recipe from Kurtic et al. (2024) and performed a W8A16 GPTQ-int8 quantization, by which we were able to largely retain the pre-quantization accuracy.

For Qwen-2.5 models, FP8-Dynamic models were created locally using LLMCompressor (Shaw et al., 2024; NeuralMagic, 2024), borrowing the same quantization recipe used by Kurtic et al. (2024) for Llama-3.1.

For BNB-nf4, we use in-flight quantization directly from the full-precision checkpoints (vLLM, 2024). We launch vLLM with quantization=bitsandbytes. This converts BF16 weights to nf4 blocks at load time,and then runs inference by de-quantizing those blocks on-chip before each GEMM, while activations remain in BF16. We do not experiment with the 8-bit integer BNB quantization (Dettmers et al.,2022) since it is not supported on vLLM.14

# A.2Using Qwen-2.5 for long context tasks:

Though Qwen-2.5 has a context length of 128K, the default configuration is set to support context lengths only up to 32K; for longer contexts, the official Qwen documentation (Qwen, 2024b) suggests employing YARN (Peng et al., 2024) to extrapolate the RoPE scaling and achieve $4 \times$ the context length. We adopt the same approach and modify Qwen model configuration when running on context lengths larger than 32K.

# A.3 Computational Cost

We estimate the approximate compute consumption as follows: NoCHA: 180O hours,RULER: 500 hours, ONERULER: 3200 hours, CS4: 180 hours, and FAcTScORE: 1OO hours, totaling roughly 5800 GPU hours on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
